rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wādī al-muqaddas means the purified valley.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {إنك بالواد المقدس} أي: المطهر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, through ʿAṭāʾ, says the valley was sanctified twice; ʿIkrima shares this view.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: (قدسته مرتين)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-Wālibī’s transmission, Ibn Abbas glosses al-muqaddas as blessed.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية الوالبي: (المقدس المبارك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary refers readers to its discussion of the sacred land at 5:21.
rows.anchor: وذكرنا الكلام في هذا عند قوله: {ادخلوا الأرض المقدسة}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Ṭuwā is the valley’s name, a view shared by all exegetes.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (هو اسم الوادي)

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan instead takes Ṭuwā to mean that it was blessed twice.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: (أي طوى بالبركة مرتين)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Hasan’s interpretation, Ṭuwā is a verbal noun from ṭawaytuhu ṭawā, meaning I folded it twice.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا (طوى) مصدر من قولك: طويته طوى.

rows.speaker: عدي بن زيد
rows.claim: The line by ʿAdī ibn Zayd uses ṭawā for something repeated upon the speaker.
rows.anchor: قال عدي بن زيد (¬8): أعاذل إن اللوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the first view: Ṭuwā is the valley’s proper name.
rows.anchor: والصحيح هو الأول

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq lists four forms: Ṭuwā with ṭāʾ vocalized either way, each with or without declension.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: ويجوز فيه أربعة أوجه، -يعني من القراءة -: ضم الطاء، وكسرها

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq explains declension by treating the name as masculine on the faʿal pattern, like Ḥaṭam and Ṣarad.
rows.anchor: فمن أجرى فلأنه مذكر سمي بمذكر على فعل نحو: حطم وصرد

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq explains nondeclension either as an altered form like ʿUmar or as a feminine place-name.
rows.anchor: ومن لم يجري ترك صرفه من جهتين أحدهما: أن يكون معدولا عن طاء

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: With kasra, Ṭuwā follows forms such as maʿā and ḍila; without tanwīn it is a place-name.
rows.anchor: قال: وإذا كسر طوى فهو مثل: معى، وضلع.

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī allows declension as a masculine valley-name or as an adjective meaning twice-sanctified, with either vowel like siwan.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي: (الصرف من وجهين أحدهما: أن يجعل اسم الوادي فيصرف

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī explains nondeclension either by a feminine locality bearing a masculine name or by alteration like ʿUmar, even from an unattested base.
rows.anchor: قال: ومن لم يصرف احتمل أمرين أحدهما: أن يكون (طوى) اسما لبقعة أو أرض وهو مذكر

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says God chose Moses for His message so that Moses would carry out His command.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (أنا اخترتك برسالتي لكي تقوم بأمري)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Listening to the revelation means acting on what God commands and forbids.
rows.anchor: {فاستمع لما يوحى} أي: اعمل بما آمرك به وأنهاك عنه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh exceeded the bounds of disobedience, committing an extreme transgression beyond that of other people.
rows.anchor: {اذهب إلى فرعون إنه طغى} أي: جاوز القدر في العصيان

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The People of Meanings supply an ellipsis: Moses was to go to Pharaoh and call him to affirm God’s oneness.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: (وفي الآية محذوف؛ لأن المعنى: إذهب إلى فرعون فادعه إلى توحيد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the command to go to Pharaoh emphasizes the order.
rows.anchor: {اذهبا إلى فرعون} تكرير الأمر بالذهاب للتأكيد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explanation of Pharaoh’s transgression was already given earlier in this sūra.
rows.anchor: {إنه طغى} قد مر في هذه السورة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One explanation from Ibn Abbas, also held by ʿIkrima and al-Suddī, is that Moses and Aaron should address Pharaoh by a kunya.
rows.anchor: {فقولا له قولا لينا} ذكر ابن عباس فيه قولين: أحدهما: (كنياه)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reported kunyas for Pharaoh are Abū al-ʿAbbās, Abū al-Walīd, and Abū Murra.
rows.anchor: واختلفوا في كنيته فقيل: أبو العباس، وأبو الوليد، وأبو مرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report describes Moses offering Pharaoh belief and worship in exchange for lasting youth, kingdom, pleasures, and eventual entry to Paradise.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى قول ابن عباس في رواية عطاء، وأبي صالح السدي عن أبي مالك

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil identifies the gentle words with the invitation to purify himself and accept guidance in 79:18–19.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: يعني بالقول اللين: {فقل هل لك إلى أن تزكى (18)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers invite Pharaoh with hope rather than certainty of success; earnest hope makes their call to truth more compelling.
rows.anchor: {لعله يتذكر أو يخشى} أي: ادعوه على الرجاء والطمع

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq, explaining Sibawayh, says God speaks in terms humans understand: Moses and Aaron act in hope though God knows the outcome, since prophets do not know the unseen.
rows.anchor: والمعنى في هذا عند سيبويه: اذهبا على رجائكما وطمعكما

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq adds that divine foreknowledge cannot itself establish the human proof; otherwise sending messengers would serve no purpose.
rows.anchor: وليس علم الله بما سيكون يجب به الحجة على الآدميين، ولو كان ذلك لم يكن في الرسل فائدة

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī reports al-Farrāʾ’s reading of laʿalla as “so that,” in keeping with the two messengers’ expectation and course of action.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: (مذهب الفراء في {لعله يتذكر} كي يتذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yafruta means to act hastily against them by punishing them; Ibn Abbas, Mujāhid, exegetes, and linguists agree.
rows.anchor: {قالا ربنا إننا نخاف أن يفرط علينا} أي: يبادر ويعجل بعقوبتنا.

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī gives the forms faraṭa, yafriṭu, furūṭan, faraṭan, and faraṭānan for acting hastily against someone.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي] (¬6): (يقال: فرط عليهم، يفرط، فروطا، وفرطا، وفرطانا)

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī says faraṭtu al-qawma means I went ahead of the people; from it come al-fāriṭ and the one who reaches water first.
rows.anchor: وقال الأصمعي: (يقال: فرطت القوم، وأنا أفرطهم فرطا إذا تقدمتهم

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī glosses al-faraṭ as haste.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي: (الفرط: العجلة، يقال: فرط يفرط)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary previously discussed this word in its explanation of 16:62.
rows.anchor: وذكرنا هذا الحرف عند قوله: {وأنهم مفرطون} [النحل: 62].

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here yatghā means to exceed the limit in mistreating Moses and Aaron.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: (أو أن يطغى) أي: يجاوز الحد في الإساءة بنا.

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī specifies the feared transgression as Pharaoh killing them.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (يقتلنا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s answer responds to their fear, and the promise to be with them means support, aid, and victory.
rows.anchor: {قال لا تخافا} جواب لقولهما: {إننا نخاف}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s promise to be with Moses and Aaron means support, aid, and victory.
rows.anchor: {إنني معكما} وعد لهما في النصرة والمعونة والغلبة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains that God hears their prayer and answers it, and sees what is intended against them and prevents it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (أسمع دعاءكما فأجيبه، وأرى ما يراد بكما فأمنع)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is not unaware of them, so they should not be anxious.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: لست بغافل عنكم فلا تهتما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some identify the sign Moses brought as the staff, while others identify it as the hand.
rows.anchor: {قد جئناك بآية من ربك} قيل: العصا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others identify the sign as the hand.
rows.anchor: قيل: العصا (¬1)، وقيل: اليد

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī says the singular āya can denote all of Moses’s signs, just as one word can denote a collection of words.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: (أراد جميع (¬3) آيات موسى، فذكرها بلفظ الواحد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: According to ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn Abbas, this is God’s blessing upon whoever follows the message Moses brought.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس: (يريد من الله عز وجل على من اتبع البيان الذي جاء به موسى)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq takes salām as safety from God’s punishment and anger for the follower of guidance, not as a greeting.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: (ليس يعني به التحية، وإنما معناه: أن من اتبع الهدى يسلم من عذاب الله وسخطه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says ʿAṭāʾ’s interpretation can mean either a greeting or Abū Isḥāq’s sense of safety.
rows.anchor: والذي ذكره عطاء يحتمل التحية ويحتمل ما قاله أبو إسحاق.

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ interprets salām as safety bestowed on the follower of guidance.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: (يريد والسلامة على من أتبع الهدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God punishes those who deny the messengers’ message and turn away; those who follow it are safe from punishment.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: {إنا قد أوحي إلينا أن العذاب على من كذب وتولى}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is called the Qur’an’s most hope-giving for believers: it says punishment is for those who deny God’s prophets and reject faith.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هذه أرجى آية (¬2) في كتاب الله للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The generic word “punishment” apparently implies that one who believes and affirms is not subject to any punishment.
rows.anchor: و {العذاب} هاهنا اسم الجنس وظاهر هذا موجب أن من صدق وآمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs shown to Pharaoh were the nine signs whose details were given earlier.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {ولقد أريناه} يعني فرعون {آياتنا كلها} يعني الآيات التسع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh treated all the signs as lies, or accused Moses of lying; he refused monotheism and called Moses a magician.
rows.anchor: {فكذب} نسب جميع ذلك إلى الكذب

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the jussive reading answers the command; the indicative is also possible as a circumstantial clause meaning the staff will swallow it.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (القراءة بالجزم (¬5)، جواب الأمر، ويجوز الرفع على معنى الحال

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī explains Ibn ʿĀmir’s indicative as a circumstantial clause of either the agent Moses or the object, the staff; the action may be attributed to its cause.
rows.anchor: وشرحه أبو علي فقال: (وجه قراءة من قرأ: {تلقف} بالرفع، وهي قراءة ابن عامر

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: For the object analysis, Abū ʿAlī allows a future action in a circumstantial clause and cites the sacrificial animal reaching the Kaʿba in 5:95.
rows.anchor: كما جاء في التنزيل: {هديا بالغ الكعبة} [المائدة: 95]

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The feminine talqafu follows the meaning of what is in Moses’s hand, namely the staff; the jussive can be command-response or an address to Moses.
rows.anchor: وقال: ({تلقف} على التأنيث، حملا للكلام على المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The magicians’ work was a magician’s trick, an illusion with no real substance.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {إنما صنعوا كيد ساحر} أي: الذي صنعوه كيد ساحر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant reads kaydu siḥr; sahir is stronger because the plot belongs to a magician, while siḥr attributes it by extension to magic.
rows.anchor: وقرئ: كيد سحر (¬4). وساحر أقوى؛ لأن الكيد للساحر في الحقيقة

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī explains kaydu siḥr as the plot of one who practices magic, like a silk shirt or brocade robe.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ: كيد سحر، أضاف الكيد إلى السحر على التوسع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the verse as saying that a magician does not prosper wherever he may be.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (ولا يسعد الساحر حيث ما كان)

rows.speaker: جندب بن عبد الله البجلي
rows.claim: Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī reports that the Prophet said to kill a magician if caught, then recited this verse and said he is not safe wherever found; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وروى جندب بن عبد الله البجلي (¬3): أن رسول الله -صلى الله عليه وسلم- قال: "إذا أخذتم الساحر فاقتلوه

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says a magician should be killed wherever found and reports that this is also the jurists’ position; al-Farrāʾ gives a similar interpretation.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (معناه حيث كان الساحر يجب أن يقتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The magicians prostrated after Moses did what he was commanded; details of the staff swallowing their work were omitted because they appear in 7 and 26.
rows.anchor: - وقوله تعالى: {فألقي السحرة سجدا} ففعل ما أمر به موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of what happened in this verse was already covered in the commentary on al-Aʿrāf.
rows.anchor: وما يقع من الكلام في تفسير هذه الآية قد سبق في سورة الأعراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion of the readings of āmantum was given earlier in the commentary on al-Aʿrāf.
rows.anchor: قد تقدم في سورة الأعراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source distinguishes prepositions: bi is used for belief in God, while li is used for belief in another, as simple assent.
rows.anchor: بوصل الباء إذا كان بالله تعالى، وإذا كان بغيره وصل باللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prepositional forms are compared with examples in 10:83, 17:90, 12:17, and 29:26; 7:123 uses bi with the same meaning.
rows.anchor: مثل قوله: {فما آمن لموسى} [يونس: 83]، {وقالوا لن نؤمن لك} [الإسراء: 90]

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains kabīr as the magicians’ teacher; Meccan usage also calls a teacher “my kabīr.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد معلمكم)

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī says a child in the Hijaz says “I came from my kabīr” when returning from a teacher.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: (الصبي بالحجاز إذا جاء من عند معلمه قال: جئت من عند كبيري)

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reads the phrase as “the greatest of the magicians.”
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن إسحاق: (إنه لعظيم السحار)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, kabīr means leader, not eldest; Joseph 12:80 calls the most knowledgeable among them their leader, hence a teacher can be called kabīr.
rows.anchor: ومنه قوله تعالى: {قال كبيرهم}

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The People of Meanings say Pharaoh portrayed the magicians’ prostration as proof they followed their chief, to turn people away from Moses.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: جعل نسبتهم إلى اتباع رئيسهم بالسجود علة لصرف الناس عن اتباع موسى

rows.speaker: المبرد، أبو عبيدة، الفراء، الزجاج
rows.claim: They explain fī as “on”: the trunks enclose the crucified men and become their place, like a house; two cited poems use this placement.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد: (المعنى على جذوع النخل، وإنما وقعت في ومعانيها الوعاء

rows.speaker: الأسدي
rows.claim: Al-Asadī’s line says graves were set above the trunks, illustrating the placement sense of fī.
rows.anchor: قال الأسدي (¬4): تداركت شماسا ويحيى وخالدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second cited line says the al-ʿAbdī was crucified in a palm trunk; the surrounding authorities use it to illustrate the enclosure sense.
rows.anchor: وأنشدوا (¬6): وهم صلبوا العبدي في جذع نخلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh says the magicians will learn who inflicts harsher and longer-lasting punishment: he for their belief, or the Lord of Moses for their refusal to believe.
rows.anchor: {ولتعلمن} أيها السحرة {أينا أشد عذابا} لكم {وأبقى}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lā is extra, yielding the question: what kept you from following me and joining me? Leaving the people could have encouraged them to leave too.
rows.anchor: - {ألا تتبعن} لا زائدة (¬2) أي: ما منعك من اتباعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that Aaron failed to follow Moses in sternly condemning the people.
rows.anchor: وقيل: (من اتباعي في الإنكار عليهم)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Aaron disobeyed by remaining among the people while they worshipped something other than God.
rows.anchor: هو قال ابن عباس: (يريد أن مقامك بينهم وقد عبدوا غير الله عصيان منك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this reading, Moses reproached Aaron for staying among the idolaters, then angrily took hold of him.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا إنما عذله على المقام فيما بينهم وقد كفروا، ثم أخذ برأس أخيه

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says Moses grasped Aaron’s hair with his right hand and his beard with his left.
rows.anchor: الكلبي: (أخذ شعره بيمينه ولحيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Moses grabbing Aaron is omitted here because another sūra mentions it; Aaron’s words themselves show Moses had taken hold of him.
rows.anchor: ولم يذكر هاهنا أخذه لذكره في سورة أخرى

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Calling him “son of my mother” rather than of their father softens the appeal and seeks sympathy, in al-Kalbī’s explanation.
rows.anchor: - {قال ابن أم} أضافه إلى الأم دون الأب ترقيقا واستعطافا

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq reports a view that Aaron was Moses’s maternal brother but not his paternal brother.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: (وقيل في هارون إنه لم يكن أخا موسى لأبيه وكان أخاه لأمه)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase is also read yā-bna-ummi with either kasra or fatḥa; the analysis was given at 7:150.
rows.anchor: وقرئ: (يابن أم) بالكسر والفتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “By my head” means by the hair of my head.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {لا تأخذ بلحيتي ولا برأسي} أراد ولا شعر رأسي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grabbing the beard was not then considered humiliating; custom treated it like taking someone by the hand, and customs affect how acts are judged.
rows.anchor: أن العادة في ذلك الزمان لم تكن كهذه العادة بل كان يجري ذلك مجرى القبض على اليد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that Moses held Aaron’s beard as he might hold his own when angry, trusting Aaron as he trusted himself.
rows.anchor: وقيل: (إنه أجراه مجرى نفسه إذا غضب في القبض على لحيته

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī says Moses thought Aaron had disobeyed God by not following him, so he seized Aaron in anger for God and to discipline him.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: (وقع في نفس موسى أن هارون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains Aaron’s fear as: if I had come to you, leaving the people behind, you would have accused me of dividing Israel.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {إني خشيت} قال ابن عباس: (يريد إن أنا أتيتك)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses Israel as the community; Aaron feared it would split into factions and fall into conflict and bloodshed.
rows.anchor: {أن تقول فرقت بين بني إسرائيل} قال ابن عباس: (يريد (¬6): جماعتهم)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron’s excuse is a plausible judgment: some would follow Moses, some stay as believers opposing the calf, and some follow al-Sāmirī, risking violence.
rows.anchor: فلا يؤمن أن يصيروا في الخلاف إلى تسافك، فاعتذر بما مثله يقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron had not kept Moses’s instruction to act as his deputy among the people.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {ولم ترقب قولي} يعني: ولم تحفظ وصيتي حين قلت لك: اخلفني في قومي

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj interprets following Moses as joining him in forcefully rebuking their unbelief and worship of other than God.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج في قوله: (ألا تتبعني) أي: في شدة الزجر لهم عن الكفر بالله

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says Aaron feared harshness would divide them into factions and make them kill one another.
rows.anchor: وقال في قوله: {خشيت أن تقول فرقت بين بني إسرائيل}: (خشيت من العنف بهم أن يتفرقوا أحزابا

rows.speaker: أبو رافع
rows.claim: Abū Rāfiʿ reports that this verse came after a Jewish seller refused the Prophet’s request to sell and lend until Rajab without collateral; the Prophet offered his armor as security and said he was trustworthy in heaven and earth. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: {ولا تمدن عينيك} الآية، قال أبو رافع

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb glosses azwājan as counterparts among the unbelievers, people alike in turning from what is right.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {أزواجا منهم} قال أبي بن كعب: (أشباها من الكفار)

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy warns that envying others’ worldly possessions brings grief, while seeing blessing only in food and drink diminishes knowledge and brings punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال أبي بن كعب في هذه الآية: (فمن لم يتعز بعزة الله تقطعت نفسه حسرات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، السدي
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and al-Suddī gloss the world’s bloom as its adornment.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {زهرة الحياة الدنيا} قال ابن عباس، والسدي: (زينة الدنيا)

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: The linguists define zahrah as the world’s brightness, freshness, and beauty, deriving it from the eye-catching blossoms of a tree.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل اللغة: (زهرة الدنيا بهجتها ونضارتها وحسنها

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq parses zahrah in the accusative as the result of what God gave them to enjoy.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (و {زهرة} منصوب بمعنى متعنا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī glosses the purpose as testing them; the author explains it as testing their gratitude for what they were given.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {لنفتنهم فيه} قال السدي: (لنبتليهم)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says God makes those worldly goods a trial for them.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: (لنجعل ذلك فتنة لهم)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reads the phrase as God’s misguidance of them by letting favor increase their disbelief and transgression; the author says this best fits the unbelievers’ condition and God’s treatment of them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (ضلالة مني لهم)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Lord’s provision refers to the resurrection.
rows.anchor: {ورزق ربك} قال ابن عباس: (يريد: في المعاد)

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī and others identify the Lord’s provision as Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي وعيره: (يعني الجنة)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The provision is greater and more enduring.
rows.anchor: {خير وأبقى} أكبر وأدوم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says that after this verse was revealed, the Prophet visited ʿAlī and Fāṭima each morning for several months and called them to prayer; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: - قوله تعالى: {وأمر أهلك بالصلاة} روي: (أنه لما نزلت هذه الآية كان رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here “your family” means the Prophet’s people and those who share his religion.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الأهل هاهنا: قومه ومن كان على دينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary refers to its earlier explanation of the verse saying that he commanded his family to pray.
rows.anchor: قوله: {وكان يأمر أهله بالصلاة}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Persevere in prayer to help resist God’s prohibitions, since prayer restrains indecency and wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: {واصطبر عليها} للاستعانة على الصبر عن محارم الله

rows.speaker: ابن مسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Muslim says God does not ask the Prophet to provide sustenance for His creation or for Himself.
rows.anchor: قال ابن مسلم: (لا نسألك رزقا لخلقنا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن سلام
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām says that when the Prophet’s household faced hardship, he told them to pray and recited this verse; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: قال عبد الله بن سلام: (كان النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- إذا أنزل بأهله ضيق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، السدي
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and al-Suddī identify the final outcome as Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقوله: {والعاقبة} قال ابن عباس، والسدي: (يريد: بالعاقبة الجنة)

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash explains li-l-taqwā as “for the people of piety.”
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {للتقوى} قال الأخفش: (أي لأهل التقوى)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the pious as those who believed the Prophet, followed him, and feared God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: الذين صدقوك واتبعوك واتقوني)

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says qaruba and iqtaraba have the same basic sense, but the iftaʿala form is more emphatic.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد: هما (¬2) واحد، إلا أن افتعل مؤكد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reckoning is near in that little time remains before it.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الاقتراب هاهنا: قصر (¬4) المدة التي بينهم وبين الحساب

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī identifies “the people” as the people of Mecca.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {للناس} قال الكلبي: يعني أهل مكة

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The exegetes take their reckoning as God’s accounting them for their deeds.
rows.anchor: {حسابهم} قال المفسرون: محاسبة الله إياهم على أعمالهم

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ, transmitting from Ibn Abbas, interprets the reckoning as punishment, since one whose account is examined is punished.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء، عن ابن عباس (¬3): يريد عذابهم: لأن من نوقش الحساب عذب

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the phrase means that the time of their reckoning has drawn near.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: المعنى -والله أعلم-: اقترب للناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this reading, the verse refers to the Resurrection, as in 54:1, “the Hour has drawn near.”
rows.anchor: كما قال في سورة أخرى: {اقتربت الساعة} [القمر: 1]

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The People of Meanings give two grounds for calling the reckoning near: everything coming is near, or it is near compared with the time already elapsed.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: واقتراب (¬2) حسابهم يحمل على أحد معنيين

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī glosses heedlessness as ignorance.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {في غفلة} قال الكلبي: جهالة

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The exegetes say the people are heedless of what God will do to them on that Day.
rows.anchor: وقال المفسرون: عما الله فاعل بهم ذلك اليوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They turn away from preparing for the reckoning.
rows.anchor: {معرضون} عن [التأهب] له

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ, transmitting from Ibn Abbas, says they turn away from what Muhammad brought.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء، عن ابن عباس: أعرضوا عما جاء به

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the alleged child of the All-Merciful refers to the angels.
rows.anchor: - قوله: {وقالوا اتخذ الرحمن ولدا} قال ابن عباس: يريد من الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God declares Himself exalted above their claim.
rows.anchor: {سبحانه} نزه نفسه عما يقولون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “honored servants” are the angels.
rows.anchor: {بل عباد} بل هم عباد يعني الملائكة.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains that God honored and selected the angels.
rows.anchor: {مكرمون} قال ابن عباس: يريد أكرمتهم واصطفيتهم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ treats the wāw as extra: the meaning is that when Gog and Magog are released, the true promise draws near; he compares 39:73 and 37:103–104.
rows.anchor: - قوله تعالى: {واقترب} اختلفوا في هذه الواو: فقال الفراء: الواو مقحمة زائدة

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī agrees that Arabs may use a semantically dispensable wāw in the response to ḥattā idhā, lammā, ḥīna, and similar temporal clauses.
rows.anchor: ونحو هذا قال الكسائي (¬1) قال: والعرب تدخل الواو في جواب (حتى إذا)

rows.speaker: امرؤ القيس
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ cites Imruʾ al-Qays’s line and takes intahā as the sense, with the preceding wāw contributing no meaning.
rows.anchor: وأنشد قول امرىء القيس (¬1): فلما أجزنا ساحة الحي وانتحى

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq rejects a dispensable wāw in Basran grammar and supplies an omitted answer to ḥattā idhā: after Gog and Magog are released and the promise nears, they say “Woe to us.”
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: والواو عند البصريين لا يجوز أن تدخل ويكون معناها الطرح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emergence of Gog and Magog is one of the signs of the Hour.
rows.anchor: وخروج يأجوج ومأجوج من أعلام الساعة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the true promise as the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: {الوعد الحق} قال ابن عباس: يريد القيامة

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī allows wa-qtarraba to coordinate with idhā futiḥat, making fa-idhā hiya shākhisah the answer to both clauses.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي (¬3): ويجوز أن يكون واقترب عطفا على "إذا فتحت"

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says hiya can be a support pronoun equivalent to huwa; the feminine agrees with the feminine word eyes, while the support pronoun may be masculine, as at 27:9 and 22:46.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء (¬4): تكون "هي" عمادا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: An Arab expression and a cited verse illustrate huwa as a support pronoun; the poem’s “fa-hal huwa marfūʿ” is another example.
rows.anchor: قال: وسمعت بعض العرب يقول: كان مرة وهو ينفع الناس أحسابهم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Alternatively, hiya anticipates al-abṣār and the later phrase explains it, an ellipsis on the condition of interpretation, as in a cited line that names the referent afterward.
rows.anchor: وإن شئت جعلت "هي" للأبصار كنيت عنها، ثم أظهرت الأبصار لتفسيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary points to its discussion of this explanatory ellipsis at 12:77.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكرنا معنى الإضمار على شريطة التفسير

rows.speaker: المبرد، سيبويه
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad, citing Sibawayh, says a masculine report takes a masculine pronoun meaning “the matter,” while a feminine report may take a feminine pronoun meaning “the story.”
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد -في هذه الآية-: قال سيبويه؛ إذا كان الخبر عن مذكر فحق الاضمار أن يكون بعلامة التذكير

rows.speaker: المبرد، سيبويه
rows.claim: The masculine construction is illustrated by 20:74 and 72:3; a feminine story-pronoun may be used for a feminine predicate, though a masculine affair-pronoun is also valid.
rows.anchor: نحو قوله: {إنه من يأت ربه مجرما}
